newsitem.title: USA: Court advisor says Liggett papers okay for trial.
newsitem.headline: Court advisor says Liggett papers okay for trial.

text.p: A court- appointed lawyer recommended on Wednesday that seven Liggett Group documents be made available to Florida state attorneys suing tobacco companies for treating sick smokers.

William Rutter, a special master appointed by the trial judge, said in his recommendation the documents contain "sufficient evidence...to support (the State of Florida's) theory of fraud" in its Medicaid anti-tobacco case.

Following two days of lawyers arguments, Rutter wrote in his opinion that the documents "substantially relate to allegations that the defendants engaged in extensive efforts to hide from and misrepresent to the public the health hazards associated with cigarettes..."
Rutter also said he found evidence that "the defendants misled and defrauded the public and public health officials regarding the relationship between smoking and health.

"There's also evidence that the defendants utilized attorneys in carrying out and planning fraudulent activities and undertook to misuse the attorney/client relationship to keep secret research and other activities related to the true health dangers of smokers," Rutter wrote.

The seven Liggett Group documents are part of the papers the small cigarette maker agreed to turn over to anti-tobacco lawyers last month in a settlement with state attorneys general seeking reimbursement for health care spending on smokers.

Rutter's recommendation now goes to the trial judge, Harold Cohen of Palm Beach County Circuit Court, for his review on Monday. If Cohen accepts the recommendations, as he ordinarily has in previous cigarette matters, then the tobacco companies could appeal Cohen's decision to a higher court.
The papers are expected to become available to the State of Florida's attorneys and the public in 60 days or less, according to W C Gentry, a lawyer representing Florida.
The seven documents date back to the early 1960s and appear to revolve around joint legal defenses among the tobacco companies, according to a log of the papers.

The papers include: an undated memorandum regarding trial strategy; a May 23, 1964, letter regarding a consumer survey; a September 18, 1981, letter, which includes notes of a meeting of tobacco company lawyers held eight days earlier; and notes from a lawyers meeting on January 23, 1981.
Rutter also found that five other documents he reviewd did not contain any information that needed to be released to the State of Florida.
On Tuesday, he released with cigarette-company agreement seven other Liggett documents, which contained information only about Liggett, a unit of Brooke Group Ltd.
